Hyperthyroid cat? Methimazole ear gel vs. pills.

If your senior cat was just diagnosed with hyperthyroidism, daily pilling may already feel like a battle. Here's what the condition is, how methimazole ear gel works, and how to make treatment easier on both of you.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 25, 2026

What is feline hyperthyroidism?

Hyperthyroidism is one of the most common hormone problems in older cats, usually those over about 10 years old. The thyroid glands in the neck, most often because of a benign (noncancerous) growth, make too much thyroid hormone. That speeds up the body. Common signs include:

  • Weight loss even though your cat is eating well, or more than usual
  • Drinking and urinating more
  • Vomiting or diarrhea
  • Restlessness, more meowing (often at night) and an unkempt coat

Left untreated, hyperthyroidism can strain the heart and raise blood pressure, so it's worth treating even when your cat seems happy.

Why methimazole is a common treatment

Methimazole blocks the thyroid from making too much hormone. It controls the condition rather than curing it, so most cats take it every day for as long as they're treated. Your veterinarian may also discuss other options, such as radioactive iodine therapy, surgery or a prescription iodine-restricted diet. Which one is best depends on your cat's health and your situation.

Ear gel, pills, liquid or chew?

Commercial methimazole tablets exist, but many cats fight pills. A compounding pharmacy can make methimazole in other forms from your veterinarian's prescription:

  • Transdermal ear gel. A measured amount is rubbed onto the hairless inner ear flap and absorbed through the skin. No pilling, and many owners find it much easier. Some cats have fewer stomach side effects this way.
  • Flavored liquid. Given by oral syringe, in flavors like chicken or tuna. A good choice for cats who take liquids well.
  • Chewable treat. For cats who happily eat treats.

Absorption through the skin can vary from cat to cat, so your veterinarian watches how your cat responds, especially after starting the gel or switching forms.

How to apply the ear gel

  1. Put on gloves or a finger cot so the medicine doesn't absorb into your own skin.
  2. Dispense the exact amount on your label from the measured dispenser.
  3. Rub it gently into the hairless inside of the ear flap until it's absorbed. It doesn't go down into the ear canal.
  4. Alternate ears with each dose if your vet says to.
  5. Wipe away old residue gently with a damp cloth before the next dose, so the skin can absorb it.
  6. Keep to the same times each day, and wash your hands afterward.
Safety for people and pets. People who are pregnant or may become pregnant should avoid handling methimazole. Keep children and other pets from touching or cuddling the treated ear right after a dose. Call your veterinarian right away if your cat has severe facial itching or scratching, yellow gums or eyes, unusual bruising, stops eating or seems very tired. Tell your vet if the ear becomes red or crusty.

Why your vet rechecks thyroid levels

Your veterinarian will usually recheck blood work a few weeks after your cat starts methimazole and after any change in dose or form, then regularly. These tests show whether the dose is right, and they check kidney values, blood counts and the liver. Hyperthyroidism can hide kidney disease, so kidney values sometimes change once the thyroid is controlled. That's why the dose is set by blood tests, not by how your cat looks.

Common questions

Does the ear gel work as well as pills?

Many cats do well on transdermal methimazole, though absorption varies. Your veterinarian checks thyroid levels to make sure it's working and adjusts the prescription if needed.

Will my cat need methimazole for life?

Methimazole controls hyperthyroidism but doesn't cure it, so it's usually given long-term. Ask your veterinarian whether a curative option such as radioactive iodine fits your cat.

Can I switch from pills to the gel myself?

No. Talk with your veterinarian first. They'll write a new prescription for the gel and recheck your cat's blood work after the switch.

This article is general information and not veterinary advice. Your veterinarian determines the diagnosis, the dose and how your cat is monitored. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved and are not commercially manufactured products.
